candidateRows: The Quran presents a unified and reasonable account in which sincere repentance, repaired harm, and predominantly good deeds lead to divine forgiveness.
This establishes the con side's affirmative account of sin, repentance, moral responsibility, forgiveness, and final judgment under the Quran.
At the outset of his opening, Ally explains the Quranic framework before turning to compare it with the biblical materials.
The Old Testament likewise teaches reward for obedience and forgiveness through prescribed offerings or sincere contrition, rather than requiring Christ's atonement.
The argument uses the Christian Old Testament to support direct forgiveness and moral accounting, challenging the necessity of the pro side's atonement model.
After outlining the Quranic view, Ally argues that Deuteronomy, Leviticus, and the prophets present obedience, repentance, and forgiveness coherently.
Neither poetic language in the Psalms nor the Genesis account of Adam establishes inherited original sin within the broader Old Testament.
Rejecting inherited original sin directly undercuts a principal premise for humanity's universal incapacity and the claimed necessity of substitutionary salvation.
Ally treats the Psalmic language as poetic and argues that Genesis depicts Adam bearing his own consequences without transferring guilt to later generations.
Paul transformed Christianity by misreading Deuteronomy's curse language and constructing justification through belief in Jesus's death apart from keeping the law.
This supplies the historical and scriptural basis for the con claim that atonement-centered salvation is a Pauline development rather than Jesus's original teaching.
Ally emphasizes Paul's early literary influence, interprets the Deuteronomic curse differently, and traces justification by faith to Paul's resulting conclusion.
Substitutionary atonement is morally and conceptually incoherent because it portrays God as punishing an innocent son or arranging a problematic payment or trap.
This is a direct coherence challenge to the pro side's central mechanism of salvation, questioning both penal substitution and alternative victory explanations.
Ally surveys substitution, divine punishment, victory over Satan, and penalty-payment accounts and argues that none provides a reasonable explanation.
The progressively later Gospel accounts modify embarrassing earlier material and increasingly portray Jesus as teaching an evolved atonement doctrine.
The proposed development weakens the pro side's appeal to Gospel testimony by treating it as a reflection of evolving Christian belief rather than stable revelation.
Using the changing treatment of Jesus's baptism and the later Lamb-of-God presentation, Ally argues that the Gospel portrait evolved over time.
Paul sometimes affirms judgment according to deeds, while James more directly contradicts Pauline justification and supports morally accountable salvation.
Internal New Testament appeals to deeds and the claimed disagreement between James and Paul support the con model while challenging Pauline consistency.
Ally cites Pauline statements about deeds and working out salvation, then characterizes James as an explicit response against Paul's doctrine of justification.
Because God's law necessarily reflects God's holy nature, forgiveness must have a ground that upholds both rather than simply suspending the law.
This gives the foundational pro rationale for atonement by arguing that direct forgiveness without satisfaction would compromise divine holiness and law.
Ally's claim that God can directly forgive sincere penitents without an atoning satisfaction.
White begins his substantive response by connecting divine law to divine nature and framing salvation as centered on God and God's glory.
Adam acted as humanity's representative, and his knowing rebellion plunged both himself and his descendants into spiritual rebellion, death, and separation from God.
The representative fall supplies the pro account of humanity's inherited condition and directly establishes the need for Christ as a corresponding representative.
Ally's argument that Adam bore his own consequences and transmitted no fallen condition to later humanity.
White contrasts Adam's original perfection with his willful rebellion and introduces federal representation linking Adam to all humanity and Christ to the saved.
Humanity is radically corrupted and falls short of God's own holiness, as shown by prophetic imagery, universal failure to love God fully, and scriptural testimony.
This contests the sufficiency of merely doing one's best by arguing that the true standard is God's holiness and that all people are morally unable to meet it.
Ally's claim that frail human beings are judged by sincere effort and predominantly good deeds rather than perfection.
White invokes dead bones, a stony heart, universal unrighteousness, the greatest commandment, and Isaiah's response to establish humanity's profound guilt.
Human beings are enslaved to sin and can come to Christ only through divine enablement, while the Son alone supplies perfect freedom and atoning mercy consistent with justice.
The move states the Christian account of human incapacity, divine initiative, liberation through Christ, and the reconciliation of mercy with justice through substitution.

After using Isaiah's response to divine holiness as the moral standard, White develops the consequence for salvation: sinners cannot free themselves, but Christ can free them and bear their sins without nullifying God's law.
Titus presents Jesus as God and Savior who voluntarily gave himself to redeem sinners, whose only adequate standing before God is Christ's righteousness received by faith.
This supplies the principal scriptural and theological case for Christ's voluntary redemptive death and imputed righteousness as the basis of salvation.

White turns from the general relation of justice and mercy to a sustained reading of Titus, arguing that Jesus is both divine Savior and voluntary redeemer, and that sinful people require another's righteousness before a holy God.
Christian good deeds do not earn or complete salvation; they result from God's Spirit purifying redeemed people and conforming them to Christ after Christ's sufficient work.
The move answers the central deeds-versus-grace issue by assigning good works a necessary transformative role without making them the ground of acceptance by God.

Continuing the Titus passage, White explains purification and zeal for good deeds as consequences of redemption, distinguishing Spirit-produced obedience motivated by love from efforts to supplement Christ's saving work.

God can forgive sins directly without violating holiness or justice, provided forgiveness reflects fair judgment rather than inequitable treatment, and mercy may extend broadly to similarly situated people.
This directly defends the opposing account of salvation by arguing that forgiveness need not require atonement and can remain just through evenhanded divine mercy.
James White's claim that direct forgiveness leaves God's law unsatisfied and separates divine justice from holiness.

Ally answers White's example of the forgiven murderer, appeals to divine prerogative and equitable mercy, and uses biblical commands to forgive debts and offenses to argue that releasing guilt does not compromise holiness.
Human beings are not absolutely depraved but can do more good than evil and may be declared righteous by God despite imperfections, as biblical examples of righteous people demonstrate.
The move contests the anthropology that makes substitution indispensable and supports salvation through accountable deeds assessed mercifully despite ordinary human shortcomings.
James White's assertion that fallen people cannot perform genuinely acceptable good and require another's righteousness.

Ally rejects total depravity, invokes the Qur'anic asymmetry between rewards for good and liability for sin, and cites Abel, Zechariah, Elizabeth, Simeon, and Anna as biblical people judged righteous without perfection.

Substitutionary justification is principally Pauline and gains support in later Gospels, while accepted datings placing Mark after Paul make Pauline influence on subsequent Christian thought historically plausible.
The move challenges the scriptural pedigree of substitution by presenting it as historical doctrinal development rather than the uniform teaching of the earliest biblical tradition.
James White's reliance on Paul, John, and Mark as mutually consistent witnesses to Jesus' substitutionary saving work.

Ally argues that White's preferred sources fit a developmental chronology, then defends post-Pauline dating for Mark by citing dates attributed to conservative Christian scholars rather than treating the position as merely liberal criticism.
Even if God enables believers to act, Paul's command to work out salvation means people must actually participate in securing their salvation and cannot rely solely on Jesus' substitutionary death.
This directly advances the accountable-deeds account by interpreting a Pauline text to require human action rather than an already guaranteed salvation resting exclusively on atonement.
James White's appeal to God's enabling work in the following Philippians verse as harmonizing good deeds with completed salvation.

Ally concedes that God may cause or assist good action but argues that the believer must still work out salvation with fear and trembling, which he says conflicts with treating salvation as already guaranteed by Christ's sacrifice.
Paul commands believers to work out a salvation they already possess, not to work for it, because God transforms saved people into a pure community zealous for good deeds.
The distinction between working for and working out salvation is White's direct resolution of the central tension between completed grace and morally necessary Christian conduct.
Shabir Ally's claim that working out salvation requires human contribution and contradicts guaranteed salvation through Christ.

At the start of his rebuttal, White distinguishes possession from acquisition: believers manifest an existing salvation as God conforms them to Christ and produces purity and good deeds, so Paul is internally consistent.
Commands for sinners to forgive one another do not show that God may forgive without atonement, because forgiven human debtors and the holy lawgiver occupy fundamentally different moral positions.
The move blocks a primary biblical analogy offered for direct forgiveness by distinguishing interpersonal forgiveness among sinners from God's response as the offended holy lawgiver.
Shabir Ally's appeal to biblical commands and prayers for interpersonal forgiveness as evidence that God can release sins without payment.

White argues that humans must forgive because they are sinners who have themselves received forgiveness, illustrating the point with Jesus' debtor parable, whereas God is neither a sinner nor a fellow debtor but the maker whose law was violated.
A discretionary or curve-based model of forgiveness risks arbitrariness, whereas Christ's perfect ransom and righteousness satisfy God's unchanging law and provide a non-arbitrary basis for grace.
This states White's principal coherence objection to direct moral accounting and contrasts it with atonement as an objective fulfillment of law grounded in God's nature.
Shabir Ally's argument that God may mercifully adjust judgment like a professor applying an equitable curve without becoming unjust.

White questions whether Ally's account permits arbitrary admission to paradise, challenges the grading-curve illustration against divine foreknowledge and holiness, and argues that believers need no curve because Christ's righteousness fulfills the law.
God's holiness and law are inseparable from his nature, so forgiveness requires a vindication of divine law rather than an ungrounded pardon.
It states the principal coherence objection to direct forgiveness and identifies vindication of divine law as the central necessity answered by atonement.
White closes his presentation by framing the dispute around whether divine law expresses God's immutable holiness and therefore must be vindicated when grave sinners are forgiven.
The repeated sacrifices of the Day of Atonement prefigure Christ's unique sacrifice, which obtains complete and enduring redemption.
The move supplies the biblical typological basis for Christ's atonement and explains why the Christian account treats his sacrifice as final and effective.
The audience question asking how Leviticus, Daniel, and Isaiah establish salvation through a sacrificial Messiah.
White connects the Levitical Day of Atonement to Hebrews, arguing that repetition exposed the sacrifices' incompleteness while Christ fulfilled their anticipated redemptive purpose.
Isaiah 53 did not predict Jesus, and the Gospel narratives were shaped retrospectively to resemble a prophecy Christians had already identified.
It directly contests the claimed scriptural foundation of atonement and contrasts Hebrews' blood requirement with Old Testament forgiveness through contrition.
White's claim that Levitical sacrifice and Isaiah anticipate and are fulfilled by Christ's final atoning sacrifice.
Ally reverses the fulfillment argument, saying later writers composed Jesus' history to match Isaiah and that the Old Testament already presents contrition as sufficient for forgiveness.
Rejecting Isaiah 53 as genuine prophecy is inconsistent with the Islamic claim that the Bible contains prophecies concerning Muhammad.
The move defends the prophetic legitimacy of a principal atonement text by applying Ally's skeptical method to Islamic uses of biblical prophecy.
Ally's contention that Isaiah 53 was retrospectively applied to Jesus rather than genuinely fulfilled by him.
White argues that Ally's method would dissolve proposed biblical prophecies of Muhammad as easily as it dissolves Isaiah's application to Jesus, producing an inconsistent standard.
The Torah and Gospel were originally revealed, but extant Christian scriptures contain later changes and acknowledged copying errors.
It establishes Ally's basis for accepting original revelation while rejecting present passages that conflict with Islamic theology, bearing directly on scriptural grounding.
White's demand that Muslims apply to the Bible the same charitable and original-language standards used when interpreting the Quran.
Ally distinguishes original divine revelation from present textual forms, citing Quranic considerations and Christian acknowledgment of copying errors to explain apparent biblical contradictions.
Quranic moral accounting makes salvation accessible because good deeds receive multiplied credit, repentance brings forgiveness, and good works erase sins.
The move positively states the Quranic salvation model and argues that Christian reliance on grace neither removes good works nor preserves a coherent legal framework.
The audience question about Islamic traditions assigning salvation or multiplied merit to particular good actions.
Ally explains asymmetric moral accounting, repentance, and sin-erasing deeds, then contrasts that account with Christianity's continuing demand for works and disputed treatment of biblical law.
Christian obedience follows the law of Christ, but acceptance before God rests entirely on Christ's perfect deeds rather than the believer's works.
It sharply distinguishes evidential obedience from the ground of salvation, supplying the core grace-based answer to Ally's claim that both systems reduce to works.
Ally's argument that Christians still need law and good deeds, making Christ's sacrifice unnecessary to the practical salvation account.
White denies that Christianity lacks law and explains that works arise from love, while peace with God and confidence of acceptance depend on another person's perfect righteousness.
If Christians remain obligated to perform good deeds and can lose salvation without them, Christ's death provides no practical advantage over direct moral obedience.
The move directly challenges the efficacy and coherence of substitutionary salvation by arguing that continuing moral obligations leave believers in the same position.
White's distinction between Christ's deeds as the ground of acceptance and Christian good works as loving, non-meritorious obedience.
Ally uses Ephesians and the continuing necessity of moral commands to argue that Christians still must do good, raising the question of what Christ's death actually changes.
Original sin and the need for a crucified savior are Pauline constructions imposed on Old Testament passages rather than teachings found in those passages themselves.
It contests both the scriptural pedigree of original sin and the necessity of atonement while offering prophetic warning and the prodigal son as alternatives.
The audience challenge that Paul's teaching on original sin and depravity in Romans rests entirely on quotations from the Old Testament.
Ally argues that neither Adam's story nor later Jewish interpretation yields inherited depravity or required atonement, and he presents Jesus' preaching and forgiveness parables differently.
Jewish diversity and messianic readings of Isaiah 53 and Psalm 22 undermine the claim that atonement was merely Paul's contextual distortion of the Old Testament.
It defends the pre-Pauline scriptural grounding of sin and atonement and challenges Ally's appeal to later Jewish nonacceptance through an Islamic comparison.
Ally's claim that Jews found no original sin or dying savior in scripture and that Paul imposed those ideas out of context.
White invokes Isaiah, Psalms, varied Jewish messianic thought, and an analogy to Jewish expectations about Muhammad to dispute Ally's historical and interpretive standard.
Deuteronomy anticipates a later prophet, whereas Isaiah 53 and Psalm 22 originally concern Israel and David rather than predicting Jesus's crucifixion.
The move directly contests the Christian claim that Israel's scriptures predict Christ's sacrificial death, a central scriptural foundation for atonement.
James White's appeal to Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, and equal treatment of Jewish expectations.
After White challenges Ally's treatment of Jewish expectations and Pauline exegesis, Ally distinguishes Deuteronomy's prophet prediction from retrospective Christian readings of Isaiah and Psalms.
Hebrews presents Jesus himself as both the offering and the superior Melchizedekian high priest, so Roman executioners do not invalidate the atonement.
This directly explains how Christ's death can satisfy the sacrificial and priestly framework despite being physically carried out by Roman authorities.
The audience objection that Roman pagans, rather than an authorized Old Testament priest, killed Jesus.
An audience member argues that a Roman crucifixion cannot constitute lawful priestly atonement; White answers from Hebrews using Jesus's enduring Melchizedekian priesthood.
The anonymous authorship of Hebrews weakens its authority, and Roman crucifixion does not match the lawful priestly sacrifice prescribed in the Old Testament.
The response attacks both the documentary authority and the claimed scriptural continuity supporting the Christian interpretation of Jesus's death as atonement.
White's claim that Hebrews authoritatively identifies Jesus as sacrifice and Melchizedekian high priest.
Following White's appeal to Hebrews, Ally argues that its unknown author supplies no secure basis for faith and that crucifixion differs fundamentally from Torah sacrifice.
Anonymous authorship does not defeat scriptural authority because Jesus used anonymously authored scriptures, and Hebrews coheres with both testaments as inspired revelation.
The move defends the authority of Hebrews, which supplies White's principal scriptural account of Christ simultaneously serving as priest and sacrifice.
Ally's contention that an anonymous Hebrews cannot reliably establish Jesus's priesthood or sacrifice.
White rejects Ally's demand for known authorship as an anachronistic isnad standard, arguing that divine inspiration, canonical recognition, and scriptural consistency establish authority.
People begin in a naturally saved condition, lose that standing by deliberate rejection, and may return through sincere repentance, restitution, and God's direct forgiveness.
This is a direct statement of the Quranic account of salvation, repentance, interpersonal repair, and forgiveness, contrasted with the necessity of transferred payment.
The audience suggestion that Islam requires people to save themselves and leaves uncertain hope of salvation.
Asked whether deeds amount to self-salvation and what happens when a victim refuses forgiveness, Ally explains fitra, deliberate estrangement, repentance, restitution, and Luke's prodigal son.
Luke cannot support forgiveness apart from atonement because its crucifixion, resurrection, Lord's Supper, and Christology govern the proper reading of individual parables.
The reply defends a canonical reading of Luke against a major con-side scriptural argument for repentance and forgiveness without sacrificial atonement.
Ally's use of Luke's prodigal son and Lord's Prayer to argue that God forgives without payment.
After Ally invokes Luke as evidence of immediate divine forgiveness, White argues that isolating those passages ignores Luke's broader presentation of Christ's sacrificial death and resurrection.
Luke does not fully adopt Pauline atonement theology, as the sacrificial wording in Luke's Lord's Supper account is a later scribal insertion rather than original text.
This supplies Ally's textual-critical basis for treating direct forgiveness as the older consistent teaching despite atonement language elsewhere in the New Testament.
White's accusation that Ally isolates Luke's parables while ignoring Luke's broader sacrificial theology.
Ally answers the contextual objection by alleging tension between Paul and earlier scripture and arguing that copyists inserted Pauline sacrificial language into Luke's supper narrative.
Jesus's sinlessness follows from his identity as the God-man and enables his sacrifice for sin, while Christian obedience results from salvation rather than producing it.
The move connects Christ's identity, sinlessness, sacrificial capacity, regeneration, and grace-based obedience in a compact account of the pro-side salvation model.
The audience request to explain why following the sinless Jesus uniquely provides eternal life and salvation.
Prompted by a comparison between sinless Jesus and a human prophet needing forgiveness, White grounds salvation in who Christ is and what he accomplished, not merely imitation.
Paul does not abolish God's moral law or teach salvation maintained by deeds; the law exposes righteousness while assurance and peace rest solely in Christ's finished work.
This extended rebuttal states the pro side's core distinction between the law's proper function, evidentiary good works, and salvation secured by Christ rather than human merit.
Ally's portrayal of Paul as abolishing Old Testament law while inconsistently requiring good deeds for salvation.
Opening his final rebuttal, White argues that Ally misreads Paul, explains the continuing moral role of law, and contrasts deed-dependent insecurity with justification and peace through Christ.
Acknowledged copying errors and divergent biblical authors defeat a presumption of unified inerrancy, whereas the Quran warrants internally coherent interpretation as a single-author work.
The move answers the methodological consistency challenge by grounding different interpretive treatment of Bible and Quran in their respective textual and compositional histories.
White's charge that Muslims inconsistently criticize biblical textual reliability while presuming Quranic inspiration and coherence.
In his closing response, Ally cites Christian admissions of copying errors, contrasts the Bible's multiple fallible authors with Quranic unity, and applies that framework to Luke's theology.
Luke's omissions and teachings on repentance indicate that he did not fully share Paul's theology of sacrificial atonement.
The argument directly challenges the claimed New Testament consensus behind salvation through Christ's sacrificial atonement.
White's claim that Paul, Luke, and the other biblical authors present a coherent theology of atonement.
After arguing that the Bible must be read as fallible writings by multiple authors, Ally presents Luke as an internal counterexample to Pauline atonement theology.
Quranic instructions concerning earlier scripture do not require Muslims to accept every word of the present Bible as divine.
This move defends the coherence of Ally's selective treatment of biblical material against a major scriptural objection.
White's contention that the Quran obliges Muslims to believe and judge by the Bible as it presently exists.
Ally interprets the cited Quranic passages as referring to prior prophetic precedent and to what God revealed within the Gospel, not to blanket biblical inerrancy.
Uncertainty about which biblical passages are genuinely divine supports turning ultimately to the Quran for authoritative judgment.
The move supplies Ally's proposed solution to the problem of mixed divine and human material in Christian scripture.
White's objection that Ally has no principled way to identify God's authentic word within the Gospel.
Ally argues that the Quran recognizes Christians' constrained situation, permits their best use of their book, and calls them toward the Quran as the final criterion.
Paul's statements about keeping the law while dismissing circumcision are internally confused and perpetuate confusion in Christian practice.
The argument attacks the coherence of Pauline teaching and contrasts it with the Quran as unified divine guidance.
White's defense that Paul continued to affirm obedience to God's law rather than rejecting it.
Ally uses circumcision as a case in which Paul's general affirmation of law conflicts with his specific teaching, then offers Quranic guidance as the resolution.
The existence of textual variants does not justify treating either scripture through a liberal reconstruction that discards its message.
The move attacks the methodological basis for Ally's differential treatment of biblical and Quranic textual variation.
Ally's claim that acknowledged copying errors in the Bible justify adopting a critical view of biblical theology.
White points to correction, replacement, and a missing page in an early Quranic manuscript, while denying that such variation licenses speculative reconstruction of the Quran.
Ally's case assumes unproved literary dependence and theological disagreement instead of allowing Paul and Luke to speak on their own terms.
This challenges the interpretive premises supporting Ally's claim that New Testament authors conflict over salvation theology.
Ally's argument that Luke followed Paul selectively and rejected key elements of Paul's atonement theology.
White says Ally employs unequal standards, assumes rather than proves authorial relationships, and builds his presentation upon a prior assumption of biblical error.
Scripture consistently teaches that holy and just God himself provides the sole means of reconciliation through Christ's accepted sacrifice and resurrection.
The move states the affirmative account of sin and salvation and grounds its exclusivity in the Bible's overarching narrative and Christ's resurrection.
White summarizes a Genesis-to-Revelation pattern of divine provision, illustrates it with the wedding garment parable, and presents the resurrection as God's acceptance of Christ's sacrifice.
An altered Quranic manuscript does not undermine the Quran because the received text has independent historical transmission through memorization and early compilation.
This directly rebuts White's attempt to establish methodological parity between textual variants in the Quran and the Bible.
White's use of corrections and a missing page in an early Quranic manuscript to challenge Ally's differing standards.
Ally distinguishes an unidentified altered copy from the Quranic text he says was memorized, written, compiled among Muhammad's companions, and dependably traced to Muhammad.
Reliance on anonymously authored biblical books creates an evidential circle unlike reliance on a Quran dependably traced to its prophet.
The argument defends Ally's unequal confidence in the two scriptures by claiming a material difference in their historical provenance.
White's claim that Ally applies inconsistent standards to anonymous biblical books and the transmission of the Quran.
Ally argues that anonymous New Testament documents cannot securely establish Jesus's acceptance of anonymous Old Testament writings, whereas the Quran has reliable prophetic provenance.
The Quran, the Old Testament, and Jesus's teaching reflected in Luke present direct forgiveness and moral accounting, while Paul teaches a departure from that pattern.
The move states the negative side's final account of sin and salvation and claims continuity for it across the Quran, Old Testament, and Jesus.
Ally closes by affirming reward for good, punishment for evil, and God's readiness to forgive, then associates that teaching with the Old Testament and Luke's Jesus rather than Paul.
